notes.h: Background: Stalin's position, the secret police and the earlier show trials
notes.b: By 1934 Stalin had already beaten every rival in the party and controlled a powerful secret police. The public trials of 1936 to 1938 copied a pattern that earlier trials had tested on engineers and foreigners.
points: Stalin had been General Secretary of the Communist Party since 1922, which let him shape the party machine and its appointments.
In the succession struggle he defeated Trotsky (expelled from the party in 1927, deported from the USSR in 1929), then Zinoviev and Kamenev, expelled in 1927 and later readmitted.

He also defeated the Right, Bukharin, Rykov and Tomsky, in 1928-29, and Bukharin was removed from the Politburo in 1929. This is why the later trials could present all of them as old enemies of his leadership.

The First Five-Year Plan (from October 1928) and collectivisation (from late 1929) brought shortages, accidents, missed targets and the famine of 1932-33. These costs created a need for someone to blame.

The secret police had passed from the Cheka to the OGPU, which was merged into the NKVD (the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs) in July 1934. The Gulag, the Main Administration of Camps, had been set up in 1930.

The Shakhty trial of 1928 tried engineers from a Donbas coal town on charges of sabotage and foreign conspiracy. The Industrial Party trial of 1930 repeated the charges against leading technical specialists, so the regime had already shown that sabotage claims could be staged.

In April 1933 six British engineers of the Metropolitan-Vickers company were among those tried in Moscow for espionage and wrecking, a case that showed the regime blaming foreigners for industrial failures.

A party purge or chistka (a cleansing of the membership) began in 1933, when members judged unreliable were expelled. In 1935 a check on party documents led to further expulsions. These purges were not at first fatal, which separates them from the Terror that followed.
notes.tip: Keep three things apart: a purge (expulsion or removal), a show trial (a public, scripted trial) and the Great Terror (the whole mass campaign of 1937-38). Examiners reward a student who can name and date each.

notes.b: Historians list several causes at once, and examiners reward ranking them. Some are about Stalin's own power, some about blame for economic failure, and some about fear of the outside world.
points: Stalin's suspicion, often called paranoia, and his wish for unchallenged personal power meant that anyone with independent standing in the party looked like a threat. This is why even loyal veterans were treated as dangerous.

Rivals: Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin were old Bolsheviks who kept the prestige of 1917 and of Lenin's time. With Trotsky in exile abroad, they could be presented as a potential alternative leadership.
Scapegoats: the costs of the plans needed an explanation other than bad policy, so managers, engineers and officials were accused of 'wrecking' (deliberate damage to industry) and sabotage.

Fear of war: as Nazi Germany and Japan grew stronger, and Hitler rose, Stalin feared a 'fifth column' (secret traitors who would help an invader), and the trials charged defendants with plotting with those powers. This is why the charges so often named Germany and Japan.
Signs of discontent inside the party: in 1932 Martemyan Ryutin circulated a platform calling for Stalin's removal, and he was expelled and imprisoned (he was shot in 1937).

The 17th Party Congress of January and February 1934, known as the Congress of Victors, celebrated the success of the plans. Of its 1,966 delegates, 1,108 were later arrested, so the Congress became a target rather than a triumph.

Historians differ on motive. Robert Conquest (The Great Terror, 1968) and Oleg Khlevniuk, working from the opened archives, stress Stalin's central direction. J. Arch Getty (Origins of the Great Purges, 1985) stresses disorder, local initiative and real tensions.

Others point to real tensions over the pace of industrialisation, fear of foreign attack, and pressure on local officials to find enemies. In short, the debate is central planning against pressure from below, and paranoia against calculation.
notes.tip: For a question on why Stalin held the trials, give causes in order of weight (rivals and power, scapegoats, fear of war), each with a dated example, and say which you think mattered most.

notes.b: The shooting of a leading Stalinist gave Stalin the pretext for the repression that followed. Whoever planned it, he used it to claim that a network of conspirators existed.
points: Sergei Kirov, party leader in Leningrad and a member of the Politburo, was shot dead on 1 December 1934 at the Smolny Institute, the party headquarters in Leningrad. The killer was Leonid Nikolaev, a young party member who had lost his job and had been briefly expelled.

A decree issued on the evening of the murder, on Stalin's initiative, ordered that terrorism cases be investigated within ten days, heard without defence lawyers, with no appeal and with death sentences carried out at once. This removed every legal protection for the accused.

The NKVD first blamed 'white guard' terrorists (supporters of the old order), then former supporters of Zinoviev in Leningrad. Nikolaev was tried in secret and shot in December 1934. This is why the blame kept shifting towards Stalin's old rivals.
Zinoviev and Kamenev were tried in secret in January 1935 and given prison terms of ten and five years. In 1936 they were brought back for a public trial on much graver charges.

Historians disagree about the murder. Conquest suspected that Stalin or the NKVD arranged it, while Getty and Matthew Lenoe (The Kirov Murder and Soviet History, 2010) find that Nikolaev acted alone. No document proving Stalin's involvement has been found.
Either way, Stalin exploited the killing. He claimed that a network of conspirators existed and that the opposition had been drawn into terrorism, and he used this claim to justify the show trials.
notes.tip: Date the murder exactly (1 December 1934) and present Stalin's involvement as a debate, not a fact. Examiners also look for Soviet accounts that use the Kirov murder as 'proof' of conspiracy, which is a sign of propaganda. Do not confuse this decree with the 1937 Order 00447.

notes.h: The first Moscow trial, August 1936: Zinoviev and Kamenev
notes.b: The Trial of the Trotskyite-Zinovievite Terrorist Centre opened the public series and showed that even Lenin's closest colleagues could be made to confess.
points: The trial was held from 19 to 24 August 1936 at the House of Unions in Moscow, with sixteen defendants led by Grigory Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev, two of Lenin's closest colleagues and former members of the Politburo.

They were charged with forming a terrorist centre under Trotsky's direction, murdering Kirov, and plotting to kill Stalin and other leaders. These charges tied the old opposition to Kirov's death, so that they looked like murderers rather than critics.

Before the trial Zinoviev and Kamenev had held out for months. Stalin reportedly promised that their lives and their families would be spared if they confessed (the source is later testimony, not a document), and the NKVD interrogators told them that confession would serve the party.

All sixteen defendants confessed in open court and were sentenced to death on 24 August. They were shot on 25 August 1936, within hours of the verdict, despite the reported promise. This is why the verdict served as a warning to every other oppositionist.

Trotsky, then living in Norway, and his son Lev Sedov were named as the organisers of the plot and were condemned in their absence. Naming him linked the accused to Stalin's chief enemy abroad, so that the plot looked like a foreign one.
Mikhail Tomsky, the trade union leader and former Right Oppositionist, was named during the trial and shot himself on 22 August 1936 before he could be arrested.
The trial opened a campaign against 'Trotskyite-Zinovievite' enemies and led to the arrest of thousands of former oppositionists.
notes.tip: Learn the first trial as: sixteen defendants, Zinoviev and Kamenev, 19-24 August 1936, all shot on 25 August. Do not mix Tomsky, a trade union leader who killed himself in August 1936, with Tukhachevsky, a marshal shot in June 1937.

notes.h: The second Moscow trial, January 1937: Pyatakov and Radek
notes.b: The trial of the so-called Anti-Soviet Trotskyite Centre moved the charges from terrorism to industrial sabotage. This gave a ready explanation for the failures of the Five-Year Plans.
points: It was held from 23 to 30 January 1937 and tried seventeen defendants, among them Yuri Pyatakov, a deputy commissar for heavy industry, and the journalist Karl Radek. This meant the trial worked as an excuse for industrial failure.

The defendants were accused of wrecking in factories and mines, causing railway accidents and plotting with Trotsky, Germany and Japan to restore capitalism. These charges explained the failures of the plans as the work of traitors.

Pyatakov testified that he had flown to Oslo in December 1935 to meet Trotsky. The Norwegian authorities stated that no foreign aircraft had landed at the airfield then, an inconsistency that foreign critics noticed.
Thirteen defendants, including Pyatakov, were shot. Radek and Grigory Sokolnikov received ten years in prison, and two others received eight years. Radek had co-operated with the prosecution.

Radek died in prison in 1939. The usual account is that a fellow prisoner killed him on NKVD orders, though the circumstances are unclear. The uncertainty is why historians describe it as 'the usual account'.
Sergo Ordzhonikidze, Commissar for Heavy Industry and Pyatakov's superior, died on 18 February 1937. The official cause was heart failure, but it is generally believed that he shot himself.
The NKVD itself changed hands. Genrikh Yagoda, its head from 1934, was replaced by Nikolai Yezhov in September 1936, and Yagoda later became a defendant in the third trial.
notes.tip: Do not write that Ordzhonikidze simply shot himself. Say the official cause was heart failure and that he is generally believed to have shot himself. Keep Radek (a journalist, second trial, prison) separate from Rykov (former head of government, third trial).

notes.h: The third Moscow trial, March 1938: Bukharin, Rykov and Yagoda
notes.b: The Trial of the Right-Trotskyite Bloc was the last and the largest of the public trials. It brought the leaders of the old Right Opposition and the former head of the secret police into the dock.
points: It was held from 2 to 13 March 1938 and tried twenty-one defendants. They included Nikolai Bukharin (former editor of Pravda and Comintern chairman), Alexei Rykov (former head of the Soviet government), the former NKVD chief Genrikh Yagoda, and Nikolai Krestinsky.

The defendants were charged with treason, spying for foreign powers, wrecking, planning to break up the USSR, and murder plots, including against Lenin in 1918, Stalin and Kirov. They were also accused of killing the writer Maxim Gorky, who died in 1936.
Yagoda and a group of doctors were accused of causing deaths by 'medical murder'.

On the first day Krestinsky denied his confession, saying it was false, but he withdrew the denial the next day after a night in NKVD hands. This shows how the NKVD could make a defendant change his mind overnight.

Bukharin admitted general political responsibility for the 'bloc' but denied the specific charges of espionage and murder. This has been read as an attempt to signal his innocence to a careful reader.

Eighteen defendants, including Bukharin, Rykov and Yagoda, were shot on 15 March 1938, and three others received prison terms. This made the third trial the most deadly of the three, with eighteen of twenty-one shot.
Bukharin was rehabilitated (officially declared innocent) by the Soviet government in 1988, as were Zinoviev and Kamenev.
notes.tip: Give the three trials with their dates and principal defendants: Zinoviev and Kamenev (August 1936), Pyatakov and Radek (January 1937), Bukharin, Rykov and Yagoda (March 1938). Do not confuse Yagoda, NKVD head 1934-36 and a defendant in 1938, with Yezhov, head 1936-38.

notes.h: How the trials were staged and confessions obtained
notes.b: The trials were scripted from start to finish, and Stalin himself oversaw the charges and the testimony. The aim was to make a confession look like proof, since there was no documentary evidence.
points: The prosecutor Andrei Vyshinsky, Procurator-General of the USSR and a former Menshevik, prepared the cases with the NKVD and argued that a confession was sufficient proof of guilt. In 1936 he demanded that the defendants be shot as 'mad dogs'.

Vasily Ulrikh, chairman of the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court, presided over all three trials as judge and helped to keep the proceedings tightly controlled. This is why the verdicts were never in doubt.

The NKVD obtained confessions by sleep deprivation, endless interrogation, threats against family members and false promises of leniency. Stalin's telegram of January 1939 confirms that physical pressure had been allowed from 1937. Such methods explain why defendants confessed to crimes they could not have committed.
The evidence for physical torture is strongest from 1937, and methods varied, so you should not say that every defendant was tortured.

Defendants rehearsed their parts. Some seem to have been persuaded that confession served the party's interest, an argument used by interrogators on loyal communists who had given their lives to the party.

The trials took place in public at the House of Unions in central Moscow before an invited audience, with foreign journalists and diplomats present and the transcripts published in several languages. The aim was to convince the world as well as the Soviet people.
Soviet newspapers and mass meetings demanded death for the 'enemies of the people' before the verdicts were given. For example, the demand for death was public before any court had spoken.

Weaknesses in the evidence were noticed abroad: the Oslo flight, a defendant's claim in the first trial to have met Sedov in 1932 at the Hotel Bristol in Copenhagen, a hotel that had been demolished in 1917, and the near-identical wording of confessions.
notes.tip: Vyshinsky was the prosecutor and Ulrikh the judge, and examiners test whether you can tell them apart. In documents questions, marks come from quoting or citing the source for each point, so make clear who was present (invited Soviet audience, foreign journalists and diplomats) so you can cite it.

notes.h: Reactions in the West and abroad
notes.b: Because foreigners were allowed into the courtroom, the trials were judged by observers who disagreed sharply. Their views are the evidence behind many documents questions.
points: Joseph Davies, the American ambassador in Moscow from January 1937, attended parts of the 1937 and 1938 trials and reported to Washington that the defendants appeared guilty. This is why Soviet propaganda could quote a foreign diplomat in the trials' favour.

The German exile writer Lion Feuchtwanger visited Moscow, attended the January 1937 trial and defended the trials in his book Moscow 1937. Ivan Maisky, the Soviet ambassador in London from 1932 to 1943, defended them to British visitors.
Western communist parties defended the trials as necessary to destroy fascist agents. Some members left the party over the issue. Their defence mattered because they were loyal to Moscow.

Some other diplomats and journalists were doubtful. Fitzroy Maclean, a junior British diplomat, attended the 1938 trial and described it later in Eastern Approaches (1949). Many liberals and socialists condemned the proceedings as a travesty of justice.

In 1937 a commission of inquiry chaired by the American philosopher John Dewey heard Trotsky's evidence at Coyoacán, Mexico, in April. It announced in December 1937 that the trials were frame-ups, and its report was published as Not Guilty in 1938.
The trials damaged the reputation of the Soviet Union among liberals and the left, at the very time of the Popular Fronts (alliances of left-wing parties against fascism).
Stalin used the verdicts to discredit Trotsky. On 20 August 1940 Trotsky was attacked in Mexico by the NKVD agent Ramón Mercader and died the next day, which ended the campaign against him.
notes.tip: The Dewey verdict (December 1937) and the book Not Guilty (1938) are two separate events, so date them separately. In source questions, say who was present, who defended the trials abroad, and whether a writer was an eyewitness or relying on hearsay.

notes.b: The destruction of the army leadership took place largely in secret, unlike the public trials. It was a closed tribunal, not a show trial, so keep the two separate.
points: Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, former First Deputy Commissar for Defence and the leading advocate of mechanised warfare, was arrested in May 1937 with other senior officers. He was a dangerous figure to Stalin because of his rank and prestige in the army.
He and seven other senior commanders were tried by a closed military tribunal on 11 June 1937 on charges of treason and spying for Germany, and were shot on 12 June 1937.
The evidence was fabricated and relied on confessions, and holding the trial in secret meant that foreign observers could not test it.

Three of the five Marshals of the Soviet Union died in the purge: Tukhachevsky and Alexander Yegorov were shot, and Vasily Blyukher died in custody in 1938. Most army commanders were arrested, as were many naval and air force officers.
Estimates of officers dismissed in 1937-38 are around 30,000 to 35,000. Many were arrested, but some were later reinstated, and political commissars regained control of the army.
The purge left the Red Army poorly led at the time of the Winter War against Finland (November 1939 to March 1940) and the German invasion of 22 June 1941.
Historians debate how much the purge explains the defeats of 1941.
Tukhachevsky was rehabilitated in 1957.
notes.tip: Say that officers were dismissed, with many but not all arrested, rather than claiming that tens of thousands were all arrested. Remember that Tukhachevsky was shot in June 1937 after a secret tribunal, not after a public trial.

notes.h: The wider Great Terror, 1937-1938: the NKVD campaign
notes.b: Show trials were the visible tip of a mass campaign run by the NKVD and carried out largely in secret. Most of its victims were not famous communists.
points: Nikolai Yezhov replaced Yagoda as head of the NKVD in September 1936, and the years 1937 and 1938 are known as the Yezhovshchina ('the Yezhov times').
NKVD Order 00447 of 30 July 1937 set quotas by region for arrests of 'former kulaks, criminals and anti-Soviet elements'. The first category was to be shot and the second sent to camps.
Local NKVD chiefs asked for higher quotas and the totals were exceeded. This is why the Terror reached far beyond the party, because local chiefs competed to show zeal.

National operations in 1937-38 targeted ethnic groups with foreign connections, such as Poles, Germans and Latvians, who were suspected of loyalty to other states. The Polish operation was the largest. This is why the Polish operation hit so many ordinary families.

NKVD records show about 1.5 to 1.6 million arrests in 1937-38 and about 680,000 executions (archives opened after 1989). Deaths in camps and prisons are additional, so some historians believe the true total of deaths was higher.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Kirov decree of December 1934 with Order 00447 of July 1937.

notes.h: The Great Terror: numbers, the party and the end of the mass phase
notes.b: The archives and Khrushchev's 1956 speech give the scale of the Terror, and its mass phase ended only when Stalin turned on the NKVD itself.
points: Many victims were ordinary workers, peasants and minorities rather than officials, so fear spread through the whole of society and not only the party.
Neighbours and colleagues were encouraged to denounce 'enemies of the people', and the families of the arrested were stigmatised and often arrested too.

According to Khrushchev's secret speech of 25 February 1956, 1,108 of the 1,966 delegates to the 17th Congress were arrested, and 98 of the 139 members and candidates of the Central Committee elected there were arrested and shot.
By 1939 the Gulag held well over a million prisoners, whose forced labour was used on the economy's projects. This shows that the Terror also fed the economy with forced labour.
The Terror slowed in late 1938. Yezhov was removed in November 1938 and replaced by Lavrentiy Beria, and Yezhov was arrested in April 1939 and shot in February 1940.
notes.tip: Give Terror numbers only as 'about' and keep camp deaths separate: about 1.5 to 1.6 million arrests and about 680,000 executions. Do not say the 1934 Congress delegates were all killed, since 1,108 were arrested.

notes.h: Key concepts in action: totalitarianism, propaganda and personality cult
notes.b: The trials show three of the syllabus concepts working together. Each one explains how Stalin could stage a lie and make people believe it.
points: Totalitarianism (a state that leaves no area of life outside political control): the secret police, the control of the courts and the press, and the ability to make leading communists confess to invented crimes show it at work.

Propaganda (the deliberate shaping of opinion): newspapers, radio and public meetings across the USSR demanded death for the 'enemies of the people', and the published transcripts and confessions were used to explain shortages and accidents.

Personality cult (the building of a leader into a heroic, near-infallible figure): the trials presented Stalin as the vigilant leader who protected the people and as Lenin's true heir, while the old Bolsheviks were written out of the revolution.

The Short Course history of the party, published in 1938, carried this further by presenting the defendants as agents of foreign powers from the beginning of the revolution. This is why the defendants could be called traitors even in the history books.
notes.tip: Higher Level essays on propaganda and terror in the dictatorships can use the trials as one example of both: public confessions are propaganda, and the NKVD is terror.

notes.h: Impact of the trials and Terror on Soviet Russia
notes.b: The trials changed every part of Soviet life: the party, the army, the economy and society. A strong answer gives a dated fact for each and ends with a judgement.
points: The party: the old Bolshevik leadership was destroyed. Stalin's rivals and potential rivals were dead or in exile, and no organised opposition was left.
Younger men promoted into the vacancies in the party, army and industry owed their careers to Stalin, which made the new elite loyal to him alone.

The army: the loss of experienced commanders, and the fear and caution in the officer corps that followed, are widely linked to the poor performance against Finland in 1939-40 and the German advance in 1941.

The economy: managers, engineers and planners were lost, and fear of being accused of wrecking made officials cautious, so they avoided decisions or falsified results. Gulag labour was used on the economy's projects.

Society: fear, denunciation and the arrest of relatives bred silence and broke families, and the families of those arrested were stigmatised as relatives of 'enemies of the people'. This is why it was safer to say nothing.

Stalin's personal power became absolute. History was rewritten in the Short Course (1938), the History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks), to make the old Bolsheviks traitors from the start and Stalin Lenin's true heir, so that no rival could claim a share of the revolution.

Later, in his secret speech to the 20th Party Congress in February 1956, Khrushchev condemned the Terror. Mass rehabilitations followed, including Tukhachevsky in 1957, and Bukharin's in 1988 was one of the last.
notes.tip: For a question on the impact of the trials, write separate paragraphs on the party, the army, the economy and society, each with a dated fact, and end with a judgement. Examiners reward linking the trials to economic failure: they explained the plans' failures as wrecking, yet the purge of managers harmed the economy.

notes.h: Assessment: the trials and the Terror
notes.b: Judgements balance the consolidation of Stalin's personal power against the damage the Terror did to the state. Examiners reward paired points and a clear verdict.
points: Achievement for Stalin: by 1939 the party, army and state were in the hands of officials loyal to him, his rivals were gone, and no organised opposition survived. This is why the Terror can be called a success in terms of power.
Limit for the regime: the loss of officers, managers and specialists weakened the army, the party and the economy in the years before the German invasion of 1941.
Contemporary supportive view: Soviet propaganda and foreign communists presented the trials as the exposure of real traitors, and visitors such as Davies and Feuchtwanger accepted the evidence.
Contemporary critical view: the Dewey Commission, liberal and socialist critics and many diplomats treated the trials as frame-ups.

Later view: after the archives opened in the 1990s, historians agree that the trials were stage-managed fabrications, though they still debate how far Stalin planned the Terror and how far it reflected paranoia or political calculation. This is why the later view differs from the contemporary views.
Later revisionist view: Getty and others stress the disorder and local initiative in the Terror, while Conquest and Khlevniuk emphasise central planning by Stalin.
Link to the economy: the trials served as the explanation of the plans' failures, since managers and engineers were blamed as wreckers.
notes.tip: Examiners reward a clear judgement with dated evidence on both sides: total control and a loyal elite for Stalin against a weakened army and economy before 1941. Do not mix Stalin's purges with Hitler's Night of the Long Knives (1934) in a comparison.

keyTerms.definition: A public trial in which the verdict is decided in advance and defendants are made to confess, so that the trial serves as propaganda.
The removal of members from a party, state or army, often by arrest and execution, to eliminate rivals or suspected opponents.
A system in which the state seeks to control every aspect of public and private life through a single party, secret police and propaganda.
The organised spread of information and images to shape opinion and promote a regime, its leader and its policies.
The promotion of a leader as an infallible and heroic figure, shown through propaganda, rituals and his image in public life.
The Soviet people's commissariat for internal affairs, which combined the secret police with the labour camp system and carried out the arrests and executions of the Terror.
The Soviet system of labour camps, administered by the NKVD, in which millions of prisoners were held and forced to work.
The campaign of mass arrests and executions of 1937 and 1938 that included the show trials, the military purge and the mass operations against 'enemies of the people'.
Members who had joined the party before 1917 and helped to make the revolution; most of those who led the opposition to Stalin were tried and shot.
The Soviet charge of sabotaging industry, used to blame managers and engineers for the failures of the Five-Year Plans.
The official clearing of the names of those wrongly condemned, begun under Khrushchev from 1956.
